dailyRead: The dollar did not need another catalyst today and it did not get one: every major moved less than 0.2% overnight, the index is 102.991 and plus 0.14%, and what happened instead is that two levels arrived at once. The first is the round number on the US curve. TradingEconomics now prints the 10-year at 5.00% on November 12, up a basis point on the session, with the last cash closes from Tuesday at 4.73% on the two-year and 5.35% on the thirty-year - Wednesday was Veterans Day and the cash market was shut. Yesterday this file wrote that the 10-year had reached roughly 4.98% and briefly traded through 5%; the honest update is that it is now simply at 5.00% and staying there, and that single number is doing the work on every other line of the board. The second level is 159.94. USD/JPY touched that overnight, its strongest in over two months, and sits at 159.759 as this is written. Yesterday this file corrected itself on the yen: 158 was not a line, and the official constraint was placed roughly 1.2 yen above spot nearer 160. That read is now confirmed by the authorities themselves. Atsushi Mimura, Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs and Japan's top currency diplomat, declined to comment on the level but said currency moves have been excessively rapid and that it is still too early to forget what happened this summer - a direct reference to the yen-buying operations run from late July into early August, one of them jointly with the United States. Japan also carried out its largest-ever yen-buying intervention around late April and early May, after the dollar climbed above 160. So the position has changed in character rather than in direction: at 158.8 the argument for a USD/JPY range was that the reward to the ceiling was small, and at 159.76 the argument is that there is essentially no reward left and the tail is an operation that historically moves the pair several yen in hours. USD/JPY stays a range, but the skew inside that range has inverted to the downside, and that is the single most important practical change on the board today. The dollar's own case is intact and also fully priced, which is why it holds at plus two rather than going to plus three. CME-based pricing has the December 9 quarter-point near 85% to 89% and the half-point bucket at roughly 11% to 15%, up from about 1% before the CPI print, after Governor Waller said a half-point should be considered if October core came in near 0.3% or higher and it did. ING's Chris Turner named 102.85 to 103.00 as big resistance for the index and it is 102.991, and the same note has EUR/USD pressing the lower end of a 1.10 to 1.15 range into year-end - it is 1.10791. Both of those are reasons to hold dollar longs rather than to add to them, and Friday's PPI at 15:30, forecast at plus 0.4% headline and plus 0.3% core against prior prints of plus 1.3% and plus 0.7%, is the last scheduled data before the vote. The second genuine reversal today is in oil, and it runs directly against what this file wrote yesterday. The claim was that the de-escalation trade had stalled and that crude had bounced off two-month lows. It has not held. WTI is 86.075 and minus 4.91% on the week, Brent is 92.440 and minus 5.95% on the week and minus 12.54% on the month, and the newest reporting attributes the fall to surging OPEC+ output alongside easing US-Iran tensions. The diplomatic record moved too: Trump has authorised Vance to negotiate with Iran with a possible Rezaei meeting under consideration, the Wall Street Journal reports Iran would allow 25 tankers through the Strait in exchange for easing the blockade on its own ports, and Iran's foreign minister says the offer to reopen the Strait within two days still stands if the war ends on all fronts. Against that, Rubio has called Iran's demands outrageous and ridiculous and said the two sides are not close, Qatar denied the reported eight-billion-dollar interim arrangement, and attacks on tankers near the Strait continue. So this is a restarted negotiation rather than a settlement - but a restarted negotiation with crude already down a fifth on the month is enough to turn USOIL from a range back to a short, and it is enough to change two currencies. It finishes the franc. CHF lost 1.99% to the dollar this week, the worst of the seven, and it goes to minus two and the bottom of the board. The mechanics are unusually clean: the policy rate is zero, Rabobank reports the consensus views a December hike as highly unlikely, the SNB itself judged in October that its threat to sell francs was no longer needed because war-induced haven flows had subsided, and its own record notes little safe-haven demand since June. A 5.00% US 10-year suppresses what is left mechanically. Yesterday this file named the reversal trigger explicitly - an oil bounce that re-bids the haven - and oil did the opposite, so the short is confirmed rather than at risk. The 1.5% October CPI is the highest in nearly three years but core is 0.5%, which says it is energy, and falling energy now removes even that. USD/CHF goes to high conviction, EUR/CHF and NZD/CHF go to high, and CHF/JPY is the cleanest short on the board at minus 0.69% on the week. It also changes sterling, and this is the correction that matters most for the open trades. Yesterday this file put December BoE pricing near 70%. The verifiable figures are lower: Bloomberg has swaps at roughly 50% immediately after the November 5 vote, up from about 30% before it and from one-in-four on LSEG data, and the most current OIS-based tracker read 58% on November 9. Bank Rate did go to 4.00% on an 8-1 vote with Catherine Mann dissenting for 4.25%, Bailey did say the rise was unlikely to be the last unless the conflict is resolved, and Deputy Governor Lombardelli said on November 10 that there is likely to be a case for a further rise in the near term. But Bailey's stated stopping condition is resolution of the conflict, and the conflict has spent this week moving toward resolution rather than away from it - FXStreet's read is that the Bank will be comfortable holding in December if energy keeps easing and oil stays below 100 dollars, with February the next hike. Oil is at 86. So sterling loses its edge from both ends at once, and it goes from plus one to zero: a coin-flip December instead of a 70% December, and the second-worst price on the week at minus 1.42% despite a 10-year gilt at 5.22% that yields more than the Treasury at 5.00%. That gilt premium is a fiscal risk premium, not a policy premium, and it is not paying the pound. GBP/AUD and GBP/NZD, both longs yesterday on the 70% figure, go to a range and a short. Today's GDP at 09:00 is the reconciliation: forecast 0.0% on the month with prelim Q3 at plus 0.7%. The upgrade on the board is New Zealand, and it is the non-obvious one. The kiwi was the best major of the week at minus 0.74% against a dollar that beat everything else by more than a percent, and the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement is now priced around 75% for a hike after the 4-3 October hold, with ANZ, Westpac and BNZ all forecasting the OCR at 3% by December and Westpac still holding a 4% peak for 2027. The September Statement itself projected exactly this - a pause in October, then 25bp to 3% in December. Yesterday this file kept conviction low on that path; the pricing says the path is the base case. The fundamentals remain the worst on the board and that is why this is plus one rather than plus two: unemployment at 5.7% is the highest since 2016, wages run 2.0% against 3.7% inflation, Q3 GDP was plus 0.2% and employment fell 0.1%. But a currency with the best price and a 75% hike is not a zero, so NZD/CHF at plus 1.25% and NZD/CAD at plus 0.96% are the two best-performing crosses on the week and both go up in conviction. Australia comes off the bottom to minus one without its case improving - it simply stopped being the worst price. AUD lost 1.37% this week against the franc's 1.99% and the loonie's 1.70%, though it is still the worst on the month at minus 2.13%. The structural cap is unchanged: the November 3 hike to 4.85% was the fifth of the year and an 18-year high, it passed 6-3 with three members preferring to hold at 4.60%, one model tracker has December 8 at roughly 78% hold against 11% hike, and markets are pricing 2027 cuts. Copper refuses to confirm the AI-demand leg at 6.2084, minus 1.05% today and minus 7.03% on the month. What keeps Australia off minus two is the highest inflation on this board, 4.3% headline with 3.6% core, and the November 17 minutes at 02:30 are the only scheduled test. AUD/NZD is where that resolves and it is now the cleanest cross trade on the board: a central bank at terminal with cuts priced for next year against one with a 75% hike and a full Statement, in a cross already minus 0.63% on the week. Canada stays at minus one and the loonie stays the second-worst price at minus 1.70%. Falling crude is the whole problem - a reopened Strait would take oil lower still and with it the case for a December 9 hike, which one estimate puts near 40%. Unemployment is 6.7%, a six-month high, employment fell 4,700 for a third consecutive monthly decline, and core at 2.2% is the softest on this board outside Japan and Switzerland. The offsetting facts are real but prospective: headline CPI at 3.1%, a Governing Council that agreed there could be a need to increase further, and the October CPI on Monday November 16 at 15:30 as the actual test. The euro is third on the board and it got there by standing still, beating five of the other six non-dollar majors while losing 1.25% to the dollar. The hike is as close to settled as these things get - ECB Watch has December 17 at 84% and Central Bank Watch at 86% as of November 11 - on October HICP at 4.0%, a three-year high, with energy up 20.8% on the year and core holding at 2.5%. The caveat worth carrying is Lagarde's own framing rather than the trackers: her line is that the Governing Council will have many indicators between now and December that will really help determine whether a hike is necessary, which is data dependence rather than a commitment, and she speaks again tonight at 21:30. The standing institutional risk, announced on October 29 rather than new today, is that she leaves on February 7, 2027, nine months early, with de Cos and Knot the names most often floated - a succession that sits directly on the far end of the 4H horizon rather than inside it. Metals are where the regime shows cleanest and where one call has to be reversed outright. Gold broke below 4,000 dollars and is 3978.43, minus 2.67% on the week and minus 4.40% on the month; yesterday's turn from a levels trade to a short was right and it goes up in conviction, with Kitco flagging 3,910 to 3,890 as the next support zone and TD Securities warning of a 3,900 retest. Silver is the reversal. Yesterday this file kept a long specifically because silver was beating gold on the week on an industrial leg that data-centre and grid demand supplies. That leg has broken: silver is 51.498 and minus 0.54% on the week against gold's minus 2.67%, which looks like relative strength until the month is read - minus 12.97% against gold's minus 4.40%. A metal falling three times as fast as gold over a month is not decoupling on industrial demand, it is being sold harder, and the one-week outperformance was noise inside that. XAG/USD flips from long to short at low-medium, and the specific fact that changed is the monthly divergence, not the daily tick. Equities are the one place where yesterday's read also needs inverting, and it is a small thing honestly stated. This file said the Euro Stoxx 50 had outperformed the DAX for three sessions on its bank weight and gave it the higher conviction. Today the DAX is 26,832 and plus 0.63% while the EU50 is 6,407 and plus 0.17%, and on the month it is plus 6.22% against plus 3.89%. The bank leg is still being paid by an 84% to 86% December hike and a steeper curve, but it is no longer the dominant leg: Brent at minus 5.95% on the week is paying the DAX's industrial and energy-input weight harder than the curve is paying the EU50's banks, and the EU50 additionally carries French and Italian political risk the DAX does not. So GER40 goes up and EU50 goes down, and the leg that decides it is energy. The one caution on the DAX is German gas, which rebounded 2.22% to 88.22 and is plus 3.43% on the month even while euro-area gas at 87.00 is minus 4.06% on the week. The practical instruction for today is narrow. The dollar is right but it is at resistance and fully priced, so hold rather than add. The two trades with the most room are the ones created by the franc going to the bottom - USD/CHF, EUR/CHF, NZD/CHF and CHF/JPY - and the AUD/NZD short. The one position to actively de-risk is any long USD/JPY: at 159.76, with Mimura invoking the summer operations and the Bank of Japan all but locked for 1.50% on December 17-18, the pair is being held up by Fed pricing alone and the asymmetry below it is now worse than the asymmetry above.

geopolitics: The de-escalation trade restarted this week, which is the reverse of what this file wrote yesterday, and it is the single fact doing the most work across the board today. Start with the record. Trump has authorised Vice President Vance to negotiate with Iran and a face-to-face meeting with Mohsen Rezaei is reportedly under consideration. The Wall Street Journal, citing Middle Eastern officials, reports Iran would allow 25 tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for an easing of the blockade on its own ports. Iran's foreign minister says the offer to reopen the Strait within two days still stands, conditional on the war ending on all fronts, and Tehran still wants the blockade lifted before talks resume. An Israeli outlet reported an interim arrangement under which Washington would lift the blockade and unfreeze eight billion dollars held in Qatar while Iran ended attacks on shipping and dropped its demand to control the Strait; a Qatari official told Bloomberg that report was false and said negotiations are ongoing, and Tehran has since rejected the asset-for-reopening framing. Against all of that, Secretary Rubio has called Iran's demands outrageous and ridiculous and said the two sides are not close to a breakthrough, attacks on vessels carrying oil and gas through the Strait continue, and Europe is reported to be negotiating its own access while the United States remains blocked. So this is a restarted negotiation, not a settlement - but a restarted negotiation is enough, because the market is trading the expectation rather than the physical flow. The price confirms it. WTI is 86.075 and minus 4.91% on the week, Brent 92.440 and minus 5.95% on the week and minus 12.54% on the month, and the newest reporting pairs the diplomacy with surging OPEC+ output as the two drivers. The gas complex is more mixed than the oil complex and the detail matters for the equity read: euro-area gas is 87.00 euros and minus 4.06% on the week, UK gas 215.71 and minus 4.09%, but German gas is 88.22 and plus 2.22% on the day and plus 3.43% on the month, so the cleanest European signal has turned the other way at the margin. Five consequences follow. First, oil goes from a range back to a short, which reverses yesterday's call and restores the consistency with a weak loonie: Canada stays at minus one, a December 9 hike sits near 40%, and analysts note explicitly that a deal reopening the Strait would push oil lower and weaken that case directly. The restraint on the short is that roughly a fifth of the barrel's value has already come out this month, so there is less premium left to drain and re-escalation is the larger tail from 86 dollars. Second, it finishes the franc, and this is the cleanest call on the board. CHF goes to minus two and the bottom. The reasoning is not the oil price itself but what the central bank has already done with it: the SNB judged in October that its threat to sell francs was no longer needed because war-induced haven flows had subsided, and its own record notes little safe-haven demand since June. With the policy rate at zero, a December hike called highly unlikely, and a US 10-year at 5.00% suppressing the residual bid mechanically, a de-escalating Gulf removes the last asymmetry the currency had. Yesterday this file named an oil bounce as the one thing that would reverse the franc short; oil fell another 4.91% instead. Third, it changes what the Bank of England's guidance means, and this is where yesterday's reading has to be inverted rather than extended. Bailey justified the November hike on a material further increase in energy prices and said the rise was unlikely to be the last unless the conflict is resolved. Yesterday that condition pointed hawkish because resolution was stalling. It now points the other way, and FXStreet's read is explicit: the Bank will be comfortable holding in December if energy keeps easing and oil stays below 100 dollars, with February the next hike. Combined with the pricing correction - about 50% to 58% rather than near-70% - sterling goes from plus one to zero, GBP/AUD from a high-conviction long to a range, and GBP/NZD from a long to a short. Fourth, the metals split along the same line and one of them has to be reversed. Gold broke below 4,000 dollars to 3978.43 because a hawkish Fed into deflating energy raises real rates, which is the one combination it cannot absorb; that short is confirmed and upgraded. Silver is the reversal: yesterday's long rested on an industrial leg decoupling it from gold, and the month says the opposite, minus 12.97% against gold's minus 4.40%. Copper at minus 7.03% on the month corroborates - industrial metals are falling harder than the haven metal, which is a demand read, not a decoupling. Fifth, the dollar needs none of this. Its case is domestic, it votes on December 9, and the CPI that settled the question covered October. It remains the only currency on the board whose path does not depend on what happens in the Gulf, which is also why its edge is now narrow rather than wide: at 102.991 against ING's 102.85 to 103.00 resistance, with 25bp at 85% to 89% and 50bp at 11% to 15%, there is very little left to discover. The equity read follows the same energy leg and flips with it. Brent at minus 5.95% on the week pays the DAX's industrial and energy-input weight harder than a steepening curve pays the Euro Stoxx 50's banks, and the relative performance confirms it - the DAX is plus 0.63% today and plus 6.22% on the month against the EU50's plus 0.17% and plus 3.89%, reversing three sessions of the opposite. So GER40 goes up to medium and EU50 down to low-medium, with energy the dominating leg and German gas at plus 2.22% the one counter worth watching.
